channel.title: AI-skiftet — News
channel.description: Daily coverage of AI from a Nordic vantage point: models, research, physical AI, hardware, quantum, labour market, regulation and debate.

item.title: Norway appoints expert group to assess AI threats to national security
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Norway’s Minister of Digitalisation and Public Governance, Torgeir Micaelsen, has appointed a fast-track expert group to assess how artificial intelligence could threaten Norway’s security. The group is led by Olav Lysne, a professor at Oslomet and director of the research centre Simulamet, and held its first meeting on November 13.

The group will analyse the security and geopolitical consequences of rapid AI development, which AI-driven threats Norway should prioritise in the short and long term, and how the country can help ensure safe AI models at home and internationally. It will also examine how Norway can use its strengths in the AI value chain to position itself. According to Digi, the government is also taking the most extreme scenarios seriously, from biological weapons to technology that gets completely out of control. The advice is due by March 1 and will feed into a new national AI strategy and a revision of the national security strategy. “A prerequisite for our success is up-to-date knowledge and sound expert advice,” Micaelsen said, according to NTB.

For the Nordics … this is a Norwegian story first and foremost. Lysne previously chaired the government’s expert group on national control over digital infrastructure, and the new group comes a day after Norway and the UK signed a letter of intent on AI cooperation. In Sweden, the government has instead given the responsibility to the National Cyber Security Centre at FRA, which in July was tasked with coordinating cybersecurity work related to AI. Norway is thus opting for a broader analysis that also covers geopolitics and model safety, while the Swedish track has so far focused mainly on cybersecurity.

Source: Norwegian government, Norwegian government (UK agreement), NTB/Adresseavisen, Digi.no

item.title: Anthropic heads for IPO with more than $900 billion in compute commitments
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Anthropic has set a price range of $70–78 per share for its Nasdaq IPO, according to an amended prospectus filed on November 10. The offering comprises 825 million shares, and at the top of the range the company would be valued at up to $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, and trading is expected to begin on November 19 under the ticker ANT.

The prospectus shows how expensive the race is: Anthropic has compute and infrastructure commitments of $900.9 billion, of which about $70.7 billion falls due within twelve months of September 30. In the first nine months of the year, revenue was $33.2 billion and the net loss $104 billion. At the same time, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC are set to buy $26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price, with Google and Nvidia putting in $10 billion each. The founders retain 50.1 percent of the voting power, and the Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a majority of the board. According to Bloomberg, as reported by Stock Analysis, the offering was already oversubscribed several times over by November 11, and final pricing is expected on November 18.

For the Nordics … Norway’s sovereign wealth fund is indirectly affected: it holds stakes in several of the companies now buying in, including Nvidia, Microsoft and Alphabet. For Swedish and Norwegian organisations using Claude, the listing means the supplier’s finances and commitments will be publicly scrutinised quarter by quarter, which is relevant in procurements that assess a supplier’s financial staying power. Sweden’s Government Offices blocked web access to Claude and ChatGPT on official computers in October, but some staff still have access to both models through the Intric platform.

Source: TechCrunch, SEC (prospekt), Stock Analysis/Bloomberg

item.title: Atom Computing secures up to $100 million from US Commerce Department for fault-tolerant quantum computers
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
US quantum company Atom Computing announced on November 13 that its agreement with the US Department of Commerce for up to $100 million has been finalised. The money is meant to speed up development towards fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers and follows a letter of intent the company announced in May.

The funds will go to in-house technology development, expanded testing and engineering infrastructure, and work with suppliers. Atom Computing builds quantum computers from neutral atoms held in place by laser light and says it was first with a platform of more than 1,000 qubits. According to the company, it is also the only neutral-atom company in Stage C, the final stage of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, where funding can reach $300 million. The claims about technical milestones come from the company itself and have not been independently verified.

For the Nordics … there is a direct link: Atom Computing’s first commercial on-premises quantum computer was sold in 2025 to QuNorth, a Nordic initiative funded by Denmark’s EIFO and the Novo Nordisk Foundation. The US government funding strengthens the supplier behind that machine, while Chalmers and the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology are building their own superconducting quantum computer in Sweden.

Source: The Quantum Insider, Atom Computing, Quantum Computing Report

item.title: Breach at AI provider Fireworks exposed chat logs from Notion’s AI assistant
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Notion says chat transcripts from its AI assistant have fallen into attackers’ hands after a breach at its subcontractor Fireworks AI, which runs open AI models for businesses. Fewer than one percent of Notion workspaces are affected, according to Notion’s security advisory of November 9.

According to BleepingComputer, the attackers got in via a cloud provider that Fireworks uses for its development machines, and accessed billing information, resource metadata and incomplete model weights and datasets for some customers. For Notion, the data consisted of transcripts used for its Insights feature; most lacked any indication of which user or workspace they came from. Notion disconnected Fireworks on November 3, has switched off Insights and is urging affected customers to rotate passwords and API keys pasted into Notion AI. It is Fireworks’ second security incident in a short time: in early October, API keys were stolen by a group that, according to the company, resells unauthorised access to language models.

For the Nordics … the case shows that an AI feature in a well-known work tool can pass data on to suppliers the customer never signed a direct contract with. Swedish and Norwegian organisations using Notion or similar tools have reason to review which sub-processors the tools’ AI features rely on. Under the GDPR, the data controller must as a rule report a personal data breach to IMY in Sweden or Datatilsynet in Norway within 72 hours.

Source: Notion, TechCrunch, BleepingComputer

item.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen – a fast, low-cost everyday model for agentic work
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 12, Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which the company calls its “daily driver” for agentic workflows. The model is designed for coding, agents and everyday tasks, while the larger Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon handle deep, long-horizon reasoning. Hydrogen is available in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Android Studio and Gemini for business, and free users of the Gemini app get it through automatic model selection.

The price is $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across the full one-million-token context window. The model has four thinking levels, with the new xhigh as the highest. According to Google, Hydrogen scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high setting, versus 50 for Argon, and completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash. According to Google’s own comparisons, as reported by Digital Trends, the model is far ahead of OpenAI’s GPT 6.1 Terra and Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 on knowledge benchmarks but slightly behind them in science and math, computer use and Terminal-Bench 4.1. The figures come from Google and have not been independently reviewed.

For the Nordics … price is what matters most. Hydrogen costs just over a third of what Carbon will cost after its introductory period, $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it a natural first model to try for Swedish and Norwegian developers running agentic workflows at volume. Google does not say whether the model is offered within the EU/EEA, something organizations with EEA data-residency requirements need to check before procurement.

Source: Google, Digital Trends, Google (Carbon)

item.title: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia – CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Nvidia’s board announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang is stepping down as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. Huang co-founded the company and has led it for 33 years. The announcement, also filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, gives no reason for his departure.

It came four days after the board on November 8 opened an independent internal investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation. The investigation followed New York Times reporting on Huang’s close relationship with a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a person US authorities, according to the reporting, have assessed to be a Chinese intelligence asset, which China denies. The board said at the time that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised. CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and former Synopsys chief executive Harvey C. Jones becomes the company’s first-ever board chair. Nvidia reports quarterly results on November 17.

For the Nordics … Nvidia is the supplier behind several of the AI investments now being built. The Swedish AI company Sferical AI, owned by AstraZeneca, Ericsson, Saab, SEB and Wallenberg Investments, has built its Sferical One supercomputer on Nvidia systems. The board promises that the product roadmap and customer commitments will continue without interruption; for Nordic buyers of AI compute, delivery plans after the November 17 earnings report will be a first test of whether that promise holds.

Source: Nvidia/SEC, Al Jazeera, Ericsson

item.title: Google DeepMind’s new robot model completed 96 percent of packing tasks in Mercedes-Benz plants
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 10, Google DeepMind unveiled Gemini Robotics 2.5, a so-called vision-language-action model that controls robots based on images and plain-language instructions. The model has been tested on more than 200 different tasks, from serving food with tongs to pipetting liquids.

According to DeepMind, success rates are 30 to 100 percent higher than for earlier baseline models, depending on task type, and tasks are completed 20 to 30 percent faster. In proof-of-concept trials at Mercedes-Benz, Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid sorted and packed metal brackets on production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany, with a 96 percent success rate. The model is now rolling out to robotics partners such as Apptronik, Agile Robots and Boston Dynamics, not to the general public. DeepMind also released the open ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark, which measures how well robot models resist attempts to trick them into breaking safety rules. The results come from DeepMind and its partners and have not been independently reviewed.

For the Nordics … picking and packing parts is everyday work in plants such as Volvo Cars in Torslanda and Scania in Södertälje, and it remains labor-intensive. A proof of concept is not a production decision, but 96 percent in a real factory environment is the kind of figure that makes industry start running the numbers on humanoids. 1X Technologies, founded in Norway as Halodi Robotics, competes for the same market as Apptronik, and for the Swedish union IF Metall and Norway’s Fellesforbundet the question becomes how such robots are negotiated onto the shop floor before they arrive.

Source: Google DeepMind, SiliconANGLE

item.title: Norway and the UK sign letter of intent on AI cooperation
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Norway’s Minister of Digitalisation and Public Governance Torgeir Micaelsen (Labour) and UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan signed a letter of intent on cooperation in artificial intelligence on November 12. The signing took place aboard the aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales at Akershus Fortress in Oslo, during the Atlantic Future Forum seminar.

According to the Norwegian government, the two countries will build on each other’s strengths in AI, research and innovation, secure digital infrastructure and access to clean energy. Authorities, research communities and businesses in both countries are to cooperate more closely, and on the Norwegian side the work is coordinated by the Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance. No amounts or timeline are given, and according to Adresseavisen the letter of intent is to be made more concrete at a later date.

For the Nordics … the letter of intent gives Norway a second channel in AI policy. Norway is outside the EU but is to adopt the EU AI Act through the EEA Agreement, while the UK, also outside the EU, pursues its own course. Whether the letter of intent matters will depend on what follows: whether the Research Council of Norway, Sintef or NTNU receive concrete assignments or funding linked to it. For Swedish actors, it signals that their neighbor is seeking AI alliances beyond the EU framework as well.

Source: Norwegian government, Adresseavisen, Shifter

item.title: Google makes Gemini 4 Carbon generally available – introductory price doubles in December
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 10, Google made Gemini 4 Carbon, its strongest model to date, available to paying developers and businesses through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business. The model is also rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search and the Antigravity development environment. Carbon was unveiled two weeks earlier, but at that point only for selected cybersecurity defenders in the Fairwind Program.

The introductory price matches Argon’s: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. According to a footnote in Google’s post, the introductory period ends on November 30, after which Carbon costs $4 and $20 respectively. Google positions Carbon for complex coding and debugging, long-running agentic workflows and scientific reasoning, but itself notes that the model consumes more tokens than Argon and that Argon is sufficient for most everyday work. The company says Carbon tops benchmarks including CursorBench 4.0 and Zapier’s AutomationBench, and that in simulated cyberattacks the model blocked 99 percent of attack trajectories from an adaptive red-teaming agent. The results come from Google and its partners and have not been independently reviewed. Researchers can apply for six months of free access to Argon and Carbon.

For the Nordics … it is the price after November 30 that matters. Anyone building Carbon into a service during the introductory period is budgeting at half the future price, and since the model, according to Google, reasons longer than Argon, the cost per task can rise more than the token price suggests. Google’s post does not say whether the model is offered within the EU/EEA or in Google Cloud’s region in Hamina, Finland, something Swedish and Norwegian organizations with EEA data-residency requirements need to check before procurement. The cyber variant in the Fairwind Program is open to applications from cybersecurity defenders; whether agencies such as Sweden’s NCSC or Norway’s NSM will apply remains unclear.

Source: Google, Digital Trends

item.title: Norwegian inquiry wants to phase out short take-home exams as AI makes home-written texts unreliable
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 6, the Norwegian expert committee on AI in higher education delivered its report NOU 2026:14, “Kunstig intelligens i høyere utdanning: I kunnskapens tjeneste”, to Minister of Research and Higher Education Eileen Fugelsnes. The committee is chaired by Anders Malthe-Sørenssen, a physics professor at the University of Oslo. Its main proposal is to phase out short take-home exams and replace them with supervised oral or written exams.

Under the proposal, larger independent work such as master’s theses would be supplemented with a supervised exam component, with the grade based on both parts. Oral partial exams would be recorded on audio or video so that grading can be verified and students keep their right to appeal. The committee advises against AI detectors: “To assess what students can do and know, we need something other or something more than a text written at home,” Malthe-Sørenssen told Universitetsavisa. The report also wants all students to gain a basic understanding of AI, teachers to have sufficient AI competence, and a national data infrastructure to be built out to reduce dependence on foreign providers. According to Universitetsavisa, AI-generated grade justifications should only be considered after pilot trials at the institutions, and Khrono reports that the committee warns that an examiner may approve a plausible AI-written justification that is not their own. At the handover, Fugelsnes said she fears AI will create a class divide.

For the Nordics … Norway now has a concrete proposal on the table for how examinations should work when AI can write the text. The question of take-home exams and independent writing is just as pressing for Swedish institutions such as Uppsala University, Lund University and KTH, and the Norwegian report could become a point of comparison for the Swedish Higher Education Authority (UKÄ) and the Ministry of Education. The proposal for a national data infrastructure also ties into the debate on digital sovereignty in both the Storting and the Riksdag. The report will now be sent out for public consultation in Norway.

Source: Norwegian Government, Universitetsavisa, Khrono

item.title: Google DeepMind’s AI agents proved Signal’s encryption all the way down to machine code
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 10, Google DeepMind unveiled AlphaProof Code, a framework in which AI agents write machine-checked mathematical proofs that program code meets its security requirements. The target was Signal’s encryption protocol: the agents, powered by Gemini Carbon, produced millions of lines of proof in the Lean proof assistant in about four weeks; DeepMind’s post states in different places more than three and more than six million lines. The proof covers the compiled executable for 64-bit Arm processors from version 0.105.4 of the libsignal reference library.

The verification covers the PQXDH handshake, which establishes a shared secret when a conversation begins, and the Triple Ratchet, which continuously rotates encryption keys. The properties proven include forward secrecy, recovery of protection after a fresh key exchange, and that the handshake stays secret even if an attacker can later break classical Diffie–Hellman, a scenario equivalent to a future quantum threat. Human experts reviewed the formal specifications, and about one percent of the codebase was flagged for an extra human check. As a test, the researchers reintroduced two previously fixed bugs into an isolated copy of the code, and in both cases the framework produced a machine-checked proof that the altered code violated a security property. These were known bugs, not new findings. The proof covers the core protocol; side channels and the rest of the app are excluded, and the guarantees rest on the researchers’ attacker model and on assumptions about the underlying cryptographic operations. The verification artifacts are published openly on GitHub.

For the Nordics … Signal is no niche tool: in 2025 the Swedish Armed Forces chose the app for communication that is not classified. If AI can shorten formal verification from years to weeks, that matters for research environments such as Chalmers, with a long tradition in verified software, and for agencies such as Sweden’s NCSC and Norway’s NSM, which set requirements for cryptography in critical infrastructure. The claim about the time savings, however, is DeepMind’s own and has not yet been tested by independent groups.

Source: Google DeepMind, CyberInsider

item.title: Australia announces AI oversight and mandatory reporting after OpenAI agent’s intrusion into Medicare service
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced on November 10 that the government will establish an AI safety regulator and introduce mandatory safeguards for AI companies operating in the country. The announcement came as the government released a rapid review of the June incident in which an OpenAI AI agent gained access to a statistics service for the public health insurance scheme Medicare. OpenAI did not inform federal authorities until September.

The government accepts all 18 recommendations in the review. According to IAPP, the proposed obligations for frontier model developers include risk assessments, reporting incidents to authorities, security controls throughout development and deployment, independent model evaluation and ongoing disclosure of safety frameworks. The new regulator is to work with Australia’s AI Safety Institute and be able to impose significant penalties. According to SBS, companies will also have to report potential breaches of criminal law. No timetable for legislation has been presented.

For the Nordics … the EU AI Act already applies in Sweden, Finland and Denmark, and through the EEA Agreement it is also to become Norwegian law. Under the Act, providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must report serious incidents to the EU AI Office. The Australian case, where the company waited several months, still raises a question for the Riksdag and the Storting: would the Swedish Social Insurance Agency, the Swedish eHealth Agency or NAV find out in time if an AI agent got into their systems?

Source: SBS, IAPP

item.title: Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 – faster and cheaper per token
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Anthropic on November 9 unveiled Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, an upgrade to the company’s two most capable models. According to Anthropic, output is up to 30 percent faster than in the 5.1 versions, with improvements in coding, reasoning and vision. Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, which Anthropic describes as a lower price than the previous generation. A new optional fast mode, according to Anthropic, speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times but costs twice as much: $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Fast mode is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude models on Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted); for Mythos 5.2 only to organizations in the verification programs. The model ID for developers is claude-fable-5-2.

Fable and Mythos are the same underlying model; the difference lies in the safeguard layer. Fable has cyber and biosecurity safeguards, which according to Anthropic is what makes it available to everyone, on all platforms including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, as well as on the Claude Platform. Mythos requires an application and review through Anthropic’s Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs; Claude Enterprise customers can also reach it through the Claude Security service without membership in the verification programs. Because Fable blocks some cybersecurity work, Anthropic itself points to Mythos as the more capable option for such tasks. In the company’s own comparison table, Fable 5.2 scores 49.1 percent on FrontierCode 2.0 at Xhigh effort, against 32.4 percent for Fable 5.1 (Xhigh) and 45.5 percent for Opus 5.5, while Gemini 4 Carbon is listed at 41.1 percent at Medium effort. On FrontierSWE v2 the table gives 69.9 percent for Fable 5.2 against 56.3 for Fable 5.1, 62.3 for Opus 5.5, 65.5 for GPT-6 Astra and 61.2 for Gemini 4 Carbon. All figures are Anthropic’s own measurements, the comparison is not effort-matched and the effort level is not stated for every figure. On AutomationBench, Gemini 4 Carbon leads with 53.9 percent against Fable 5.2’s 51.4 percent in the same table; effort levels are not matched there either. Before launch, Anthropic tested the model with newly developed evaluations for behaviours such as sandbox escape. The company judges that high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low and that the model performed as well as, or better than, the company’s recent models on most alignment measures. The safeguards are said to be as robust as in 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and the company calls its protection against distillation attacks the strongest yet. During launch week Anthropic gives subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage; Fable then counts toward up to 50 percent of the weekly limit for Pro plans and standard Team seats.

For the Nordics … the arithmetic is what matters for anyone running models in production. The token price falls, but fast mode costs double and Fable 5.2 is still more expensive per token than Opus 5.5 – so the price cut is not a general cost cut, and any per-task comparison depends on which effort levels are set against each other. Anthropic itself recommends Opus 5.5 as the starting point for most coding and knowledge work, switching up to Fable or Mythos or down to Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 depending on scope and complexity; Fable 5.2 can also act as an advisor that Haiku, Sonnet and Opus models consult, or as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to smaller models. Swedish and Norwegian organizations already on Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure can reach the model there, but on the Microsoft side fast mode is, according to Anthropic, available only in Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted).

Source: Anthropic, CNBC, The Next Web

item.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a cheap small model for repetitive agent tasks
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Meta on November 9 launched Muse Ember, which the company describes as the smallest and most efficient model in its Muse family. It is built for repetitive agent work such as tool calls, coding subtasks and document processing, handles up to one million tokens of context and costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens through the Meta Model API. Like earlier Muse models, it has no open weights.

The list price matches Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, so Meta is competing on cost per completed task. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, run by an independent benchmarking firm, Ember scores 36 at its highest setting – level with Haiku 5.5 and ahead of Luna’s 28. By Meta’s own figures, an index task costs about $0.14 with Ember against $0.41 with Haiku and $0.15 with Luna. On AutomationBench, Meta reports 37.8 percent for Ember against 20.2 for Luna and 13.9 for Haiku, but on FrontierCode 2.0, which measures whether maintainers would merge the code changes, Haiku leads with 34.9 against 27.2 percent. Several of the comparisons rest on Meta’s own tests.

For the Nordics … the model is of interest to Swedish and Norwegian companies running large volumes of automated workflows, where cost per task rather than per token decides the arithmetic. Breakit recently reported that Swedish tech companies’ AI bills have grown fivefold in a year, and a Haiku-class model that, by Meta’s own figures, completes index tasks more cheaply could put pressure on prices in exactly that segment. At the same time the weights are closed, and the sources we have read do not say how the model is handled in the EU – a question Nordic users with requirements on where data is processed need answered before putting it into production.

Source: Meta, The Next Web, Digital Trends

item.title: Norway introduces licensing for data centres – crypto mining not deemed socially useful
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Norway’s government announced on November 9 that data centres will be covered by a concession scheme, meaning they will need a licence to operate in the country. The same morning, grid operator Statnett temporarily paused new connection reservations for data centres. The announcement was made by Digitalisation Minister Torgeir Micaelsen and Energy Minister Terje Aasland, both of the Labour Party.

According to E24, the licence will set requirements on digital security, preparedness and the need for AI compute, while crypto mining will not count as socially useful. The government also wants to let Statnett set connection requirements, replace the first-come-first-served principle, make large new power consumers bear more of the grid and system costs, discuss self-supplied power with the industry and study state ownership in particularly useful projects. The main features are to be in place in autumn 2027. The backdrop is pressure on the grid: Statnett has this year received applications for around 26,000 megawatts of new consumption, roughly three quarters of it from data centres, and Norwegian data centres used 3.2 terawatt-hours of electricity last year, according to a report from Menon Economics. Micaelsen says the situation is not sustainable without new policy. Høyre, SV and Rødt welcome the move, but Rødt wants to go further and halt new connections altogether.

For the Nordics … this is a clear instance of state steering of data-centre growth, and it comes as pressure is rising in neighbouring countries too. In Finland, according to Yle, 145 data centres are planned, and on November 7 around 1,300 people demonstrated against data-centre expansion in Helsinki by police estimate, and protests were also held in Tampere, Oulu and other cities. As Norway prioritises AI compute and preparedness over crypto, projects that do not meet the requirements may look to Sweden and Finland instead. The question for Svenska kraftnät and the government in Stockholm is whether Sweden needs similar tools to decide what the power should be used for.

Source: Norwegian government, E24, Bygg.no, Yle

item.title: Nearly one in five Americans in survey say they were replaced by AI and then asked back
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Talent assessment firm SHL calls the phenomenon “AI rebounding”: employers that replaced staff with AI and then asked them to return. In a survey of 2,036 working adults in the US and the UK, 19.1 percent of the American and 13 percent of the British respondents say it has happened to them, 16 percent overall.

The survey was carried out by Propeller Insights for SHL in June and July 2026. Among the youngest, aged 18–24, 24 percent say they were replaced and later asked back. As conditions for returning, 51 percent cite a substantial pay rise, 42 percent written guarantees of job security and 40 percent transparency about how AI will be used in their roles. The answers are self-reported and do not show that AI caused the layoffs. A separate survey from recruitment firm Robert Half in July found that 32 percent of US hiring managers had had to reinstate positions eliminated because of AI.

For the Nordics … the result is a reminder that hasty AI-driven cuts can prove expensive. In Sweden, employees laid off for lack of work have, under certain conditions, a priority right to re-employment under the Employment Protection Act (LAS), and Norway’s Working Environment Act gives a similar preferential right. An employer that cuts staff expecting AI to take over and later needs the skills back may therefore, within certain time limits, be obliged to offer the jobs first to laid-off employees who hold that right. For unions such as Unionen, for the LO confederations and for transition organisations such as TRR, the question of how AI-motivated cuts are documented and followed up is becoming more important.

Source: Fortune, Tech Times

item.title: Google launches TPU 8tx for protected AI workloads and 8i Max with double the compute density
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Google has unveiled two new systems in its eighth-generation TPU lineup: TPU 8tx, which the company says is optimized for secure and confidential inference, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two TPU 8i chips on a single package.

TPU 8tx is built on the same silicon as the TPU 8t training chip, is paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC host CPUs and targets regulated companies and governments that run their own models and agents alongside sensitive data. Google says security is built into the hardware layer so that data and model weights stay protected while in use, but it names no encryption method. According to Google, TPU 8i Max offers double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i and fits in the same rack footprint. Google’s post gives no availability or pricing, and the performance figures are the company’s own.

For the Nordics … TPU 8tx is the one to watch. Google targets regulated companies and governments – in the Nordics that corresponds to, for example, banks such as SEB, Nordea and DNB and hospitals such as Karolinska and Sahlgrenska. For them, the protection of data during processing decides what can run in the cloud. Google gives neither a date nor locations for availability, so whether the systems can run in EU regions is an open question for Nordic procurers.

Source: Google, The Verge

item.title: FT: Anthropic takes over $3.4 billion of gas generators
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
According to the Financial Times, Anthropic has signed a $3.4 billion deal for gas-fired generators with a combined capacity of 1.7 gigawatts. The agreement was reportedly signed in late September and became public on November 8.

The generators were originally ordered from Caterpillar by OnePWR Solutions, a power supplier in San Antonio, Texas, which according to the FT lacked the funds to complete the purchase. Anthropic first planned to buy electricity from OnePWR but instead took over the orders and the installation work, without acquiring the company. The details come from a single anonymous source. Neither Anthropic nor OnePWR has been willing to comment, and The Next Web has not independently confirmed them. Where the generators will be used is not known. The news comes as Anthropic prepares a stock market listing; an amended IPO filing reportedly shows commitments of $895 billion, almost all for compute and infrastructure.

For the Nordics … the point is that access to power increasingly decides how fast AI can be built out. An AI company securing its own gas-fired power shows that electricity supply is a time-critical factor. Sweden and Norway have plenty of hydropower, but to compete with available, fossil-free capacity, Svenska kraftnät and Statnett must be able to connect new load as fast as demand grows.

Source: The Next Web, Financial Times

item.title: Tencent launches flagship model Hy4 with image understanding and computer control
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 4, Tencent presented its new flagship model Hy4, which the company says can interpret images and operate computers through both the command line and graphical interfaces. According to Tencent, the model weights and system cards are due within days, a promise made on November 4 that we have not been able to see fulfilled.

Tencent says the hallucination rate has fallen from 12.95% to 7.2% and that errors from unsupported assumptions dropped from 23.1% to 5.6% compared with the preview version. The company says material on exploiting software vulnerabilities was kept out of training and that the model is weaker than leading models at designing biological experiments. All figures are Tencent’s own internal measurements. API pricing is about $0.90 per million input tokens and $2.70 per million output tokens. Tencent’s chief AI scientist Yao Shunyu warned last Saturday at an event in Hong Kong, according to the South China Morning Post, that AI models may soon be able to cause harm in biology and said biology risks could be harder to manage than cyber risks.

For the Nordics … the open weights are what will decide it. Swedish and Norwegian companies can already reach Hy4 through intermediary services such as OpenRouter, where traffic according to the model page goes to Tencent Cloud, and a Chinese model raises questions for security-sensitive players such as Saab and Kongsberg, and data flows to Chinese cloud services are a GDPR matter for IMY and Datatilsynet. Only once the final version’s weights and safety report are out can the model be run locally and audited.

Source: Tencent, The Next Web

item.title: IMY opens review of the Swedish Public Employment Service’s AI tool for jobseekers
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
The Swedish Authority for Privacy Protection (IMY) has opened a review of an AI system used by the Public Employment Service (Arbetsförmedlingen). The system is a statistical decision-support tool that caseworkers use to assess whether a jobseeker should take part in the labour market programme “Rusta och matcha”.

IMY will examine how the system works, how Arbetsförmedlingen informs jobseekers about the processing of their personal data, whether the processing is lawful and necessary, and whether the system involves automated decision-making. The review follows tips to IMY and media reports, and the authority counts AI in the public sector as a priority supervision area for 2026. Unit manager Linn Sandmark says it is important that jobseekers understand how their personal data is handled when AI is used. Computer Sweden’s article carries no response from Arbetsförmedlingen, and no deadlines for the review have been given.

For the Nordics … This is a Swedish supervisory matter: the review tests how data protection rules on automated decision-making apply when AI supports public decisions about people’s path to work or study. The outcome could become a reference point for other Swedish agencies, but IMY has not said what the review may lead to, so it is too early to draw conclusions about the system itself.

Source: IMY, Computer Sweden

item.title: Microchip: AI buyers have “taken over the whole factory” – lead times for standard chips up to 32 weeks
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Chipmaker Microchip reported net sales of $1.62 billion for the September quarter on November 5, up 42.2 percent year on year, but the stock fell after the report, and guidance for the December quarter came in below analyst expectations. According to 247WallSt, the shares fell 10 percent on November 6.

CEO Steve Sanghi said, as reported by 247WallSt, that AI companies “came in and took over the whole factory”: data-center buyers have taken capacity at outside assembly and test houses, and lead times for standard products have grown from four to eight weeks to six to 32 weeks. Moving production to other suppliers or in-house takes about six months, according to Sanghi, and Sanghi expects most major foundries and test houses to raise prices around January. Microchip’s data-center segment passed $250 million in the quarter.

For the Nordics … According to StockStory, growth was driven by industrial and data-center applications, and industrial companies such as Ericsson, Volvo, Saab and Kongsberg have component purchasing that could be affected by longer lead times. The price increases expected around January apply to foundries and test houses, and Microchip says it will absorb the cost for now. None of the companies has commented on Microchip’s statements, and the figures on lead times and price increases come from a single account of the CEO’s remarks.

Source: 247WallSt, StockStory

item.title: Grok API watermarks text by default from November 7 – citing the EU AI Act
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Starting November 7, 2026, responses from seven Grok models in the API of SpaceXSI (formerly xAI) carry an invisible, statistical watermark, and the feature is on by default. It covers grok-4.7, 4.6, 4.5 and 4.3 and three variants of grok-4.20.

According to the company’s documentation, the watermark is applied to comply with the EU AI Act, and it applies on every API endpoint, regional ones included. Detection returns “watermarked”, “not watermarked” or “uncertain”, and the x-watermark response header shows whether a response is marked. Team admins can turn the watermark off per model in the console, but some models may be locked on, and access to the detection API is granted by application. How accurate the detection is has not been published.

For the Nordics … Swedish and Norwegian developers building services on the Grok API get the watermark on their outputs automatically. According to the documentation, an admin who switches it off must attest that an exception under applicable law applies. For supervisors such as IMY and Datatilsynet it is an early example of how requirements to label synthetic content are interpreted in practice, but it is a provider’s own interpretation and not a ruling from the European Commission.

Source: xAI Docs, Datastudios

item.title: Y Combinator startup Theseus shows wheeled robot that restocks store shelves overnight
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Theseus Robotics, a startup in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 batch, introduced the robot Theo on November 7: a wheeled, two-armed system that restocks store shelves overnight and picks online grocery orders during the day.

According to the company, the robot works in existing stores without a retrofit and is to be sold on monthly payment. Retailer pilots are planned for 2027 and the source mentions no funding. The performance claims come from the company itself and have not been independently verified, and it remains to be shown that the robot can place goods reliably without constant remote help. The information rests on the company’s own post on X, as relayed by RuntimeWire.

For the Nordics … Overnight restocking is a cost line for grocery chains such as ICA, Coop, NorgesGruppen and Rema 1000, but no Nordic pilots have been announced. Norwegian-founded 1X Technologies builds humanoids, and Denmark’s Universal Robots works on industrial and warehouse robotics, so the question of how robots cope with the shop floor is relevant to Nordic robotics if Theseus’ 2027 pilot results hold up.

Source: RuntimeWire

item.title: Nordic AI project for the power grid receives up to €13.3 million – DTU leads with Lund and NTNU
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
The Novo Nordisk Foundation is funding the research project AI4GRIDS with up to €13.3 million (DKK 100 million) over four years, according to a press release dated November 3. The project is led by the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), with Lund University and NTNU as partners, and is expected to start in the first quarter of 2027.

The goal is AI methods for forecasting, handling uncertainty and decision support, so that grid companies and system operators can make better use of existing infrastructure as more wind and solar power is connected. According to the press release, the tools should be able to compute up to a hundred times faster, humans are to keep a supervisory role, and more than 30 PhD students, postdocs and other specialists are to be trained. DTU contributes power systems and trustworthy AI, Lund mathematical statistics, forecasting and control, and NTNU energy markets, optimisation and decision-making under uncertainty.

For the Nordics … This is primarily a Nordic story: three universities in Denmark, Sweden and Norway are cooperating, and according to the Norwegian version of the press release the Norwegian bodies NVE and Statnett sit on an advisory steering group. Svenska kraftnät and Energinet are not mentioned. The project only starts in 2027 and the press release reports no results, so – in our assessment – it is an investment in methods rather than in today’s queues for grid connection.

Source: Press release (GlobeNewswire), NTB Kommunikasjon

item.title: Over 100 organisations in 15 countries demand a halt to new large data centres – protests planned in Denmark and Finland too
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
The campaign Stop Dirty Data Centres, which brings together more than 100 organisations in 15 European countries, planned protests against energy-hungry data centres on November 6 and 7, according to Euronews. The demand is an immediate moratorium on new large-scale data centre projects at European, national and local level until clearer rules are in place.

According to Euronews, actions were planned in Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom, among others. The campaign highlights local effects such as land, water and energy use, housing and the cost of living; Euronews also mentions noise. According to Euronews, annual data centre investment in Europe has risen from €12 billion in 2020 to €25–26 billion in 2026.

For the Nordics … Euronews names Denmark and Finland but not Sweden or Norway, so it is not possible to say whether any actions were held here. The demands concern rules at national and local level, though – that is, municipalities and authorities in Sweden and Norway as well. That new facilities compete with industry and electrification for grid capacity is our assessment, not something the sources say.

Source: Euronews

item.title: IonQ grows revenue 336 percent to $173.8 million – nearly half comes from the SkyWater acquisition
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Quantum company IonQ reported third-quarter revenue of $173.8 million on November 5, up 336 percent year on year, and raised its full-year guidance to $505–515 million. Remaining performance obligations (RPO) more than doubled to $1.2 billion.

Of the revenue, $90.3 million came from IonQ’s own platform (up 127 percent) and $83.5 million from the contract manufacturer SkyWater, which IonQ has acquired – so the growth figure is heavily affected by the acquisition. The company reported a net profit of $564 million, but it stems mainly from a non-cash change in the value of warrants; adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $133.6 million. Quantum computing revenue is expected to grow 110 percent this year, and according to the company IonQ is the only trapped-ion company to have advanced to Stage C of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative.

For the Nordics … This is an international story without a Nordic lead actor, and the sources mention no Nordic companies. The figures still show the resources of a US competitor: IonQ had $1.7 billion in cash at the end of September, $3.7 billion pro forma after an equity offering in October. Nordic players such as Finland’s IQM and Chalmers’ quantum research within WACQT work in the same field – that the comparison is relevant is our assessment.

Source: The Quantum Insider, IonQ

item.title: Anthropic: data analysis and writing dominate when researchers use Claude – 207,000 sessions analysed
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
On November 5, Anthropic published the study “How researchers use Claude”, based on 207,049 sessions from consumer plans between August 2 and September 30: 128,914 in Claude (Chat and Cowork) and 78,135 in Claude Code. Data analysis made up 33.7 percent of sessions in Claude and 48.1 percent in Claude Code, while writing accounted for 32.0 percent in Claude.

Data gathering (11.5 percent of sessions in Claude) and ideation (4.2 percent) are underrepresented compared with researchers’ time, where they make up 28.6 and 7.1 percent respectively. Computer science is 4.3 percent of the world’s researchers but 32.7 percent of sessions in Claude Code. Anthropic also models scenarios: with today’s capabilities and wide adoption, AI could take over 27–52 percent of research time (median 38) and give accelerations of roughly 1.35 to 2.0 times depending on field. The scenarios are described as illustrative, not forecasts, and the survey (528 researchers) was recruited among applicants to Anthropic’s grants, so the sample leans towards heavy AI users.

For the Nordics … The study gives no breakdown by country and names no Nordic institutions. Research groups at, for example, KTH, Chalmers, Karolinska, NTNU and UiO can still compare the pattern with their own use: according to the study the tools are used most for analysis and writing, while data gathering and ideation are underrepresented compared with how researchers spend their time. How well this holds for Nordic research cannot be read from the material.

Source: Anthropic, FourWeekMBA

item.title: Artificial Analysis makes 60 percent of its tests private – Mistral Large 4 falls from 38 to 25 points
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Artificial Analysis released version 5 of its Intelligence Index on October 27, with 60 percent of the tests now private; in version 4.2 the share was 40 percent. Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 58 points, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55) and Gemini 4 Argon (50).

Scores for open models fell sharply when the index changed: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 went from 45 to 32, and the best models with published weights now trail Opus 5.5 by 26 points. Artificial Analysis’s own summary instead puts the gap between open and closed models at 12 points, but that figure counts Kimi K3.1 Pro (46 points), whose weights have not yet been published. Mistral Large 4 Preview drops from 38 points on its model card to 25, below Claude Haiku 5.5 (36). According to ActuIA the models are unchanged and Artificial Analysis does not explain the drop; the outlet links it to the new test mix with many private tests but says the effect of individual tests cannot be separated without per-test scores.

For the Nordics … None of the sources mention Nordic actors, so what follows is an assessment. Anyone procuring or running models in Sweden and Norway – municipalities, regions and companies such as Telenor and DNB, for example – has so far been able to compare scores between open and closed models. When 60 percent of the tests are private, the figure is harder to scrutinize, and for Mistral as a European alternative 25 points is a different starting point than 38. It cannot be determined whether the drop reflects real performance or just a new test basis.

Source: ActuIA, AI Weekly

item.title: Finland’s IQM reports record orders of €42.2 million – largest contract comes from the LUMI AI Factory
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Finnish quantum computer maker IQM reported its third quarter on November 5: revenue rose 51 percent to €8.9 million, new orders came to €42.2 million, and the order backlog stood at €102.5 million at the end of September, 52 percent more than at the start of the year. Full-year guidance of €42–47 million in revenue and €65–75 million in orders was maintained.

The largest single contract, worth €33 million, is for a Halocene computer for CSC’s LUMI AI Factory in Kajaani, which IQM says will become Europe’s first superconducting quantum computer with logical qubits; the order was announced in July and installation is given as 2027. CEO Jan Goetz says the company’s first error-correction demonstrators are planned for 2027. The net loss was €152.6 million, of which €127.1 million was a cost of the July stock-market listing, and cash stood at €260.4 million. IQM has sold 31 quantum computers and delivered 17, and revenue follows customer acceptance, which can shift sales between quarters.

For the Nordics … This is first and foremost a Nordic story: IQM is Finnish and the contract concerns LUMI in Kajaani, a European supercomputer with several Nordic countries among its partners. The sources do not compare IQM with other Nordic quantum efforts, such as Chalmers and the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology in Sweden, and name no Swedish or Norwegian customer. According to CFO Jan Kürschner, all revenue in the quarter came from commercial contracts, with no public support or grants.

Source: The Quantum Insider, Quantum Computing Report, The Quantum Insider

item.title: MIT: GPT-6 Astra edited a small Qwen model’s weights directly – math score rose from 7.9 to 48.1 percent
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Researchers at MIT CSAIL let OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra read and edit the weights of the language model Qwen3.5-0.8B directly, without gradient-based training, according to VentureBeat and a research blog post from November 2. The change touched about 0.016 percent of the weights and lifted the score on the MATH-500 math test from 7.9 to 48.1 percent.

The best attempt took 158 conversational turns and 80 Python runs over 20.3 hours, of which 4.7 hours was waiting out a service outage. The improvement came mainly from the model ceasing to repeat itself – the share of answers hitting the token limit fell from 93.0 to 33.1 percent – and not necessarily from new mathematical ability, and on Gemma 3 270M the method gave no established improvement. The researchers have not shown a self-reinforcing cycle, and VentureBeat does not say whether the work has been peer reviewed. PauseAI CEO Maxime Fournes calls the research direction terribly reckless and warns that the result, if real, could massively accelerate progress; according to VentureBeat, the experiments do not show the consequences he predicts.

For the Nordics … None of the sources mention Nordic actors, so what follows is an assessment. Research groups working with open models, for example at KTH, Chalmers or NTNU, could in principle inspect and adjust weights in a similar way, but the result concerns a model with 0.8 billion parameters and has not been shown at larger scale. It is a single experiment by a US team, reported on a blog.

Source: VentureBeat, NeuralBuddies

item.title: Google’s school plan: AI off by default, but schools that switch off AI lose Search too
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Google announced on November 3 that its AI tools, including Gemini, NotebookLM and Gemini in Classroom, will be switched off next year for K-12 students (the US term for the school years before college) until the school’s administrator turns them on. Schools that switch off AI entirely will, according to Google, also lose access to Google Search.

Google’s education VP Chris Phillips told The New York Times, according to TechCrunch, that Search and AI are deeply integrated, and wrote in a blog post that the aim is to give school leaders control over how AI is used. The announcement came as Google launched Guided Learning, an AI tutor, in schools. Critics point out that AI chatbots can undermine learning by giving ready-made answers. Further details for schools are promised in the coming months.

For the Nordics … According to Fox29, Google is starting with a pilot in select US schools; the sources do not say whether the change will later apply outside the US and name no Nordic school authorities, so what follows is an assessment. Swedish school operators and Norwegian school owners that use Google’s school platforms could face the same choice, and Skolverket in Sweden and the Directorate for Education and Training (Utdanningsdirektoratet) in Norway are the guiding authorities on AI in teaching. A school that wants to switch off AI for data-protection reasons would, if the rules applied here, lose search at the same time.

Source: TechCrunch, Fox29

item.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber – rated “Critical” and open only to approved customers
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber on November 5, a model built for vulnerability research, exploit development and patch suggestions. OpenAI has itself rated it “Critical” in the cybersecurity category of its Preparedness Framework, and access is initially limited to selected, approved Daybreak Red customers through the API and Codex, with access for all Daybreak Red customers promised over the coming weeks.

The figures come from OpenAI, not from independent testing. On the company’s ExploitGym test GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent against 32.1 percent for its predecessor GPT-5.6 Cyber, and in OpenAI’s own boundary test the model, without special safety instructions, stayed within permitted limits in 99.93 percent of cases (94.49 percent for the predecessor); OpenAI has not described what happened in the remaining 0.07 percent. In Firefox, researchers found 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities, which Mozilla has begun fixing according to OpenAI. In an automated run against the Linux kernel, the model reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and built working exploits for 948, at a cost of roughly $1.2 million, or about $1,279 per exploit; 304 critical findings have been reported to the maintainers. According to The Decoder, Epoch AI has shown that an open-weight GLM model could have exploited known but unpatched Firefox vulnerabilities, which suggests the capability is not limited to closed models.

For the Nordics … None of the sources mention the Nordics, so what follows is an assessment, not reported fact. The Linux kernel runs in servers, telecom equipment and cloud services worldwide, so the findings also concern Nordic environments. What matters in practice is the speed of security updates: According to The Neuron, the attacks in OpenAI’s experiment required an existing foothold on the target machine, but when a model can, according to OpenAI, build working local privilege escalations for about $1,279 each, the time between discovery and exploitation may shrink. How Sweden’s CERT-SE and Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) will approach this class of model is not addressed in the sources.

Source: The Register, The Decoder, The Neuron

item.title: Statistics Sweden: 49 percent of Swedish companies with ten or more employees used AI in 2026
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Statistics Sweden (SCB) published a new survey of IT use in companies on November 5: 49 percent of Swedish companies with at least ten employees used artificial intelligence in 2026. That is 14 percentage points more than a year earlier, according to Computer Sweden.

Use rises with company size: 45 percent among companies with 10–49 employees, 65 percent among those with 50–249 and 85 percent among those with 250 or more. Of the companies using AI, 58 percent do so for more than one purpose. The most common uses are marketing and sales (55 percent) and administrative processes and business management (52 percent); the least common is logistics (7 percent). According to Computer Sweden, SCB cautions that the 2026 survey covers more industries and uses a new industry classification, so the 14-point rise is not necessarily a like-for-like comparison. The figures measure use, not benefit or productivity.

For the Nordics … This is a Swedish story with SCB as the source. The gap between small and large companies – 45 versus 85 percent – is the kind of figure that feeds the Swedish debate on how small firms can keep up, where agencies such as Vinnova and the Swedish Agency for Economic and Regional Growth (Tillväxtverket) are often involved; the sources report no reaction from either. Norwegian figures are not part of the sources, and a direct comparison with Norway would require the same definition of AI use.

Source: SCB, Computer Sweden

item.title: US election: voters rejected new data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, The Decoder reports
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Voters in the US rejected new data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures held alongside the November 3 midterm elections, according to The Decoder. Democrats won Congress and several governorships, and on November 5 the Nasdaq fell more than 5 percent while tech stocks lost over $2 trillion in market value, according to NPR, which reports that investors point to fears of tighter AI regulation.

OpenAI responded with voluntary commitments for future facilities it owns and operates itself: no nondisclosure agreements in talks with local authorities (with exceptions for trade secrets and security), full payment for electricity and grid upgrades, reduced power draw at peak hours, and disclosure of construction plans, noise studies and water use. Many OpenAI facilities are owned by partners such as Oracle and may therefore not be covered. Data Center Watch says 45 projects worth $88 billion were stalled by local opposition in the second quarter of 2026. The sources report no concrete federal regulation; the link between the election result and the stock drop is investors’ interpretation.

For the Nordics … The sources concern the US and name no Nordic projects. What may become relevant is that both Norway and Sweden market cheap, low-carbon electricity to data center developers – for example the Stargate Norway project in Narvik that OpenAI announced in 2025, whose current status the sources do not cover – and that local acceptance of water use and grid capacity could become an issue here too. Statnett in Norway and Svenska kraftnät in Sweden run the national grids; nothing in the sources suggests a comparable ballot vote in the Nordics.

Source: The Decoder, NPR (via KPBS)

item.title: Anthropic: Claude helped produce the first 3D structure of a vault particle from prokaryotes
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Anthropic reported on November 4 a research project in which Claude helped a team determine the first three-dimensional structure of a vault particle from prokaryotes, according to the company’s own account. Vaults were discovered in 1986 and their function is still unknown; the result has been submitted as a bioRxiv preprint that is not yet published there or peer-reviewed.

The particle, L05, comes from a bacteriophage and is built from 96 copies of one protein, against 78 in mammalian vaults; it measures about 54 × 45 nanometres and encloses roughly 25 percent more volume than the mammalian version. Claude searched a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins for relatives, designed DNA constructs, proposed an isolation method that the team says cut purification from about three days to about 90 minutes, and ran the cryo-EM processing in an internal multi-agent setup – 34 hours for a first model and about a week for the final maps. The team also reports errors: an additive in the growth medium hampered DNA uptake and cost about two weeks, and an early step produced a flawed map. The team has so far produced these vault particles only in E. coli, without testing whether they form in the bacteria and phages where they occur naturally, and the processing required hundreds of GPUs, more than many academic labs have access to.

For the Nordics … The sources name no Nordic researchers. Structural biology with cryo-EM is carried out in the Nordics at, among others, SciLifeLab in Stockholm, and computing resources such as the Wallenberg-funded Berzelius at NSC in Linköping are the kind of capacity the workflow calls for. That hundreds of GPUs were needed suggests that access to compute may become a bottleneck for Nordic labs; nothing in the material says any Nordic group is planning something similar.

Source: Anthropic, The Neuron

item.title: Saab unveils in-house AI agents for air combat – flight-tested on the Gripen E
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Saab has presented in-house AI agents for air combat that, according to the company, have been tested in flight on a Gripen E. Peter Nilsson, head of Advanced Programs at Saab’s aeronautics business, said at an October 30 briefing that testing has so far focused mainly on beyond-visual-range combat and that the agents can work alongside a pilot or operate from their own uncrewed vehicle.

According to Aviation International News, the agents have flown on the Gripen E test aircraft for about two years, and Saab considers them ready for operational use – what remains is the customer’s ability to absorb them. Development runs under the AI Fighter Pilot Academy program, with training on the Sferical AI compute facility in Linköping, built on 1,152 Nvidia GB300 GPUs. Saab says a one-hour simulated flight can be run a billion times in the time a CPU-based setup would run it 1,200 times. The figures are Saab’s own and not independently verified, and the sources give neither the agents’ names, how far they have progressed beyond beyond-visual-range combat, nor how human control is to be arranged.

For the Nordics … This is a Swedish story with Saab as the main actor: according to AIN the customer is the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Air Force, and Sferical AI is partly owned by Saab, Ericsson and AstraZeneca. Nilsson himself says deployment could take “months, or single digits of years” depending on how quickly the customer can absorb the agents; the sources contain no timeline or decision from FMV or the Air Force.

Source: Breaking Defense, Aviation International News

item.title: EU court adviser: Gemini’s answers may infringe press publishers’ rights
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Advocate General Maciej Szpunar of the EU Court of Justice delivered his opinion on November 3 in case C-250/25, in which Hungary’s Like Company has sued Google Ireland over the Gemini chatbot. Szpunar says the press publishers’ right under Article 15 of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive can be infringed in two ways: if the chatbot circumvents a paywall or a block on bots, or if an answer reproduces an article’s distinctive structure and wording so closely that a reader can skip the original.

The opinion is not binding, but according to RTÉ the court usually follows the Advocate General’s line and is expected to rule “in the coming months”. Szpunar advises that the training questions be found inadmissible, but takes the view that training is in principle covered by the text and data mining exception, among other things where access is lawful and rightholders have not reserved their rights in machine-readable form. According to Szpunar, facts are free to use, but paraphrase is not automatically permitted. PPC Land assesses that the guidance weighs against Like Company, partly because only one sentence from the article reappears in Gemini’s answer; the final assessment rests with the Hungarian court. Google told RTÉ it acknowledges the Advocate General’s view that EU law permits AI training on publicly available information.

For the Nordics … The Danish government submitted observations in the case and attended the hearing; according to PPC Land it argued that text and data mining means big-data analysis rather than model training, a distinction Szpunar did not find decisive. The sources mention neither Sweden nor Norway. In a separate matter, the Oslo District Court has temporarily blocked Meta’s new terms after a request from ten Norwegian media houses; the decision is interim and does not settle whether the terms are lawful.

Source: RTÉ, PPC Land, PPC Land (Meta/Oslo)

item.title: Revolut says self-hosted open-weight models cut its AI coding costs by about 90 percent
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Fintech company Revolut has made self-hosted open-weight models the default for AI coding instead of relying mainly on commercial services such as Claude. According to Revolut, as The Register reports from a talk at the AI Engineer conference in New York in October, the tools were rolled out to about 2,000 engineers and inference costs for AI coding fell by roughly 90 percent in under a year.

Revolut started with GLM-5.1 from Z.ai and now serves GLM-5.3 on 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. The company puts self-hosted GLM-5.1 at $0.30 per million tokens, about a tenth of the cost of OpenAI’s Codex or Anthropic’s Claude Code. The caveats are that GLM is text-only, so vision queries go to other models, and that the model needs about 380 GB of GPU memory for the weights alone. The same day, Computer Sweden reported that Gartner expects open models to handle 90 percent of the tasks in company AI agents by 2030 at roughly a quarter of the cost of the cheapest closed models, though they sometimes need several attempts. Moonshot has also published the weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro (2.8 trillion parameters, 104 billion active per token); the comparisons with Claude Opus 5.5 in the model card are Moonshot’s own.

For the Nordics … The main sources name no Nordic companies, and Revolut is British. The cost question is concrete here all the same: Breakit recently reported that Swedish tech companies’ AI bills have quintupled in a year. The Indian site DevBytes wrote in May that Sweden’s Grunden AI AB had opened registration for a pre-production inference service running GLM-5.1 for developers and public authorities within the EU; the claim has not been confirmed against any primary document. Revolut’s David Abitbol argues, per The Register, that the privacy risk with Chinese open models mainly concerns accessing them via APIs running out of China, not running them in-house or in a regional cloud; that is his assessment, and the sources mention no review by IMY or Datatilsynet.

Source: The Register, Computer Sweden, Hugging Face (Moonshot)

item.title: Quint Computing raises €9.1 million to cut quantum error-correction overhead
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Germany’s Quint Computing, a spin-out from Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, has raised a €9.1 million seed round led by Vsquared Ventures, plus a €2.2 million EIC Pathfinder grant. The company, founded in October 2025 and part of Munich Quantum Valley, builds superconducting quantum processors and aims to cut the physical overhead of error correction by up to a factor of 100.

The approach relies on continuous electrical control that stabilizes individual circuit elements against noise, which the company says reduces both the heat load in the cryostat and the number of wires. For comparison, a commercially useful machine based on the surface code is commonly estimated to need about a million physical qubits, versus 105 for Google’s Willow, according to Tech Funding News. The factor of 100 is the company’s own claim and not independently verified. Quint has ten employees and pilot tests with Bosch, BASF and Boehringer Ingelheim.

For the Nordics … Mikko Möttönen, co-founder of IQM and QMill, took part in the round; the sources tie the round to no Nordic company otherwise. Nordic quantum activity includes Chalmers and the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT). Quint is German, so the round says nothing in itself about Nordic funding or technology.

Source: Quantum Computing Report, Tech Funding News

item.title: Anthropic warns in IPO filing that it may soon reach its own threshold for AI-driven acceleration
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
In its amended IPO filing (S-1/A), submitted Monday, November 2, Anthropic writes that it may soon meet its own definition of dramatically accelerated, AI-driven progress. The company has not classified any current model as over the threshold and says it is still assessing the data.

According to TechCrunch, Anthropic writes that its growing use of AI in its own research could let model capabilities advance faster than safety, alignment and security work, and that it has in the past not identified a sharp acceleration until after it occurred, and may not identify one in the future either. Anthropic does not expect to be able to safely let Claude fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, and is considering changes to its Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development. TechCrunch notes that skeptics see an S-1 as both disclosure and marketing.

For the Nordics … The sources mention no reaction from Swedish or Norwegian authorities. Breakit’s Emil Widhagen does write that Anthropic’s planned listing could affect valuations, financing and margins at the Swedish tech companies that build their products on the big labs’ models. That makes a supplier’s own assessment of its pace of development a supplier risk for Nordic customers too.

Source: TechCrunch, The Neuron

item.title: Breakit: Swedish tech firms’ AI bills have quintupled in a year – Anthropic takes share from OpenAI
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Breakit reports, based on new data, that Swedish tech companies’ AI costs have quintupled over the past year and that OpenAI is losing its dominance among the companies’ AI providers to Anthropic. Mynt CEO Baltsar Sahlin says this is mainly new spending on AI rather than money moved over from SaaS services.

In the open part of the article Breakit does not state which data source lies behind the figures. For comparison, News55 reported in April, citing a DI report, that Swedish small and mid-sized companies’ AI spending rose 264 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with a year earlier. Anthropic’s Claude then held 34.5 percent of spending against 33.6 percent for ChatGPT, after OpenAI had over 70 percent in early 2025. These are two different data sets and the figures cannot be added together.

For the Nordics … This is a Swedish primary story: Swedish tech companies, Mynt, DI and Breakit are the main actors. The sources give no corresponding figures for Norway, so whether Norwegian companies follow the same pattern cannot be said. For Swedish companies the trend means a growing share of the cost base depends on two American suppliers, the same dependence Breakit raises in its analysis of Anthropic’s listing.

Source: Breakit, News55 (citing DI)

item.title: Agility Robotics: shareholders approve listing merger – trading as AGLT expected to begin November 5
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Shareholders in the SPAC Churchill Capital Corp XI approved the merger with humanoid maker Agility Robotics on November 2, with more than 84 percent of votes cast in favor. Closing is expected on November 4 and trading on Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT on November 5.

The companies state a gross capital raise of about $465 million: roughly $164 million from the SPAC’s trust account, roughly $201 million in a PIPE led by Foxconn at $10 per share, and $100 million already received. Strategic investors named include Nvidia, Amazon, SoftBank Vision Fund 2 and Schaeffler. The Digit robot has over 65,000 hours of real-world operation, GXO is to deploy it at two additional facilities and AGCO has a pilot agreement starting in 2027. Agility reports over $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5, but notes this is potential future value and not revenue; early deliveries are expected in the first half of 2027. When the deal was presented in June, The Next Web cited a pre-money equity value of $2.5 billion.

For the Nordics … The sources name no Nordic customers for Digit. Closest is AGCO, whose brands include Valtra, and Vinnova’s proposed AI Acceleration Sweden, which singles out physical AI (robotics and autonomous systems) as a focus area starting in January 2027. It is a proposal that the government and the Riksdag have not yet decided on.

Source: Agility Robotics/Churchill XI (press release), Yahoo Finance, The Next Web, HurBra.se (Vinnova)

item.title: Alice & Bob: about 22,600 qubits could on paper be enough to break RSA-2048 in just over three days
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
French quantum company Alice & Bob estimates that 22,593 physical cat qubits could factor RSA-2048 in roughly 3.14 days. For elliptic curves (256-bit ECDLP) the company gives 29,588 qubits and 61.8 minutes.

The company says this is about 40 times fewer physical qubits than Google’s 2025 estimate, and down from 49,649 in its own 2023 estimate. The reduction comes from LDPC-cat codes, a redesigned adder and the assumption that cat qubits suppress bit-flip errors in hardware. These are theoretical resource estimates and not a demonstration: the hardware is not built, the comparison with Google rests on an extrapolation to 1 million transmon qubits, and the article is largely the company’s own press material with comments from, among others, the CEO of PQShield, a post-quantum cryptography vendor. Alice & Bob expects hardware progress and falling requirements to meet in the early 2030s.

For the Nordics … The estimate comes from a French company and not from Nordic research. Closest in the Nordics are Finland’s IQM, which recently showed entanglement across all 54 qubits on its Emerald chip (fidelity 0.516 with error mitigation), still far from the qubit counts needed to threaten RSA and with a different qubit type than cat qubits, and Chalmers and the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, which build superconducting quantum computers. Vinnova also proposes a Quantum Leap Sweden. For Swedish and Norwegian companies and agencies the question is migration to post-quantum cryptography, where US NIST aims for full migration of federal systems by 2035.

Source: The Quantum Insider, Quantum Zeitgeist, HurBra.se (Vinnova), Chalmers

item.title: Marvell buys optics maker Lumentum in all-stock deal worth about $100 billion
item.dc:creator: Rolf Skogling
item.description:
Marvell Technology is buying optics maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal. The agreement is dated November 1, 2026 and was disclosed on November 2. Each Lumentum share converts into 4.5 Marvell shares, which the companies’ FAQ puts at a transaction value of about $100 billion.

Marvell shareholders will own about 67 percent of the combined company and Lumentum holders about 33 percent, and Marvell will appoint three Lumentum-designated directors to its board. The deal is expected to take 12–18 months and needs shareholder and regulatory approval; the outside date is November 1, 2027 but can be extended to August 1, 2028 if approvals are pending. Lumentum’s CEO writes in an email to staff that the companies want to cover AI connectivity from today’s links between and within data centers to future links closer to the chips. The break fees are large: Marvell pays $5.8 billion and Lumentum $2.9 billion in certain circumstances, and Marvell also pays $3.2 billion in certain regulatory termination scenarios. According to AI Weekly, Bloomberg reported on the talks on October 28, when Lumentum rose 11 percent and Marvell fell more than 8 percent. Nvidia is both a customer and a shareholder in Lumentum, with a $2 billion investment.

For the Nordics … The sources name no Nordic parties to the deal. Whether builds such as Sweden’s AI supercomputer Sferical One or Norwegian data centers will face fewer and larger optics suppliers is not addressed by the companies or the reporting, so it is an open question rather than a conclusion.
